items.title: Philippines: Flood Control Project Disregards Rights
items.description: (Manila) – Philippine authorities disregarded the rights of residents who were removed from a small island in Pampanga province for a flood control project and relocated to a site with chronic flooding and few livelihood opportunities, Human Rights Watch said today. In 2022, the Macabebe, Pampanga government relocated 90 families without adequate consultation and information from Pulo Island on the Pampanga River. The relocation site, in the town of Macabebe, is a low-lying area that was formerly a fish pond that floods throughout the year, causing residents to struggle to access services and work. Although the Pulo community wanted to stay together, some family members have since left because of the effects of the flooding on their lives and livelihoods. “Philippine authorities in Pampanga have threatened the safety and livelihoods of Pulo Island residents by relocating them to a low-lying area as part of a flawed flood control project,” said Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The Philippine government should consult the community to find a better solution and ensure that future relocations related to flood control projects respect affected people’s rights.” Play Video Pampanga province in the Philippines’ northern island of Luzon experiences the country’s most severe flooding, which is exacerbated by storms, sea-level rise, and limited dam capacity, and is likely to worsen as climate change accelerates. From 2015 to 2025, floods and sea-level rise displaced 6.6 million people in the Philippines. The Philippine government has adopted a national policy for moving entire communities, called planned relocation or resettlement. However, the authorities responsible for moving the Pulo Island community did not follow national or international standards to protect affected people’s rights. Planned relocations, according to the United Nations Guidance on Protecting People from Disasters and Environmental Change through Planned Relocation, should be a measure of last resort to protect life and health, and based on consultation with affected communities or at their request. One of the community boats used to ferry people during the day’s most flooded time at the Pulo relocation site, July 12, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Some residents built elevated houses anticipating frequent flooding, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Aidaliza Aquino supports her husband, Eduardo Aquino, who uses a walker for mobility, at the Pulo relocation site in Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, Pampanga, Philippines, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The river tide reached 1.6m during the high point of flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Human Rights Watch interviewed 35 residents of the Pulo relocation site in Pampanga’s Barangay Candelaria, Macabebe, between July and August 2026, as well as 9 authorities in Pampanga, and climate change experts. Human Rights Watch also analyzed satellite imagery of Pulo Island and the relocation site, and employed photogrammetry—using a camera to obtain precise measurements—to determine the difference in elevation between the relocation site and the dike. Between 2020 and 2023, the Pampanga municipal government and the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) dredged Pulo Island and relocated the island’s residents. Human Rights Watch found that the relocation did not involve adequate consultation, access to information, or the selection of a suitable site. “They removed us [from Pulo Island], and they put us in a place where we feel we were thrown here like trash,” said a 48-year-old mother of two children. Ria Clarin looks out to water surrounding her house, her daily view since moving to the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Ria Clarin’s house is unfinished because floodwater occasionally enters her house despite added elevation at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Mallari’s home at the Pulo relocation site was built without elevation, allowing flood waters to enter her home every day, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Residents like Evangeline Bansil have a pair of rain boots for daily wear due to flooding at the Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The community boat that ferries people across the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 13, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Public works department engineers told Human Rights Watch that the late mayor of Macabebe, Anette Balgan, had requested the dredging—excavating sediment, soil, and other material from the bed of the Pampanga River—and to relocate the community. They said that removing the island would increase the river’s capacity and prevent flooding in the area, making the relocated residents and communities along the river safer. Beginning in 2018, government officials held several meetings with the affected families, some in the local Kapampangan language. None of the residents interviewed by Human Rights Watch felt they were given a choice about the relocation. Community members said they were informed about the relocation site in 2021, and expressed concerns about its suitability during meetings with authorities. The relocation site is below a dike, an elevated ridge built parallel to the river bank to prevent floodwaters reaching nearby residential areas. A road runs along the top of the dike beside the relocation site and serves as the main route to the town. “They did not present any other solutions,” said the 48-year-old mother. “There were no options.” Longtime residents said they felt pressured to move without understanding the reasons, or the compensation and assistance being provided. Residents were required to demolish their own homes to receive compensation. Many feared that if they did not demolish their houses quickly enough, the funding allocated would run out, based on rumors spread in the absence of official information. Some said they felt intimidated by the authorities. “The personnel on site were slightly harassing us too, telling us that we are obligated to leave, that we have no choice, and that they will tell on us to higher authorities,” said a 57-year-old farmer. Evangeline Bansil and Rina Tolentino wade through thigh-deep flood waters, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch The level of the river reached 1.6m during high tide at the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A resident looks out to water, her daily view in the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Maria Luz Suñga stands in front of her home at the flooded Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch A man carries a boy on his back as they wade through floodwater around the Pulo relocation site, July 14, 2026. © 2026 Lian Buan/Human Rights Watch Many of the families are related and wanted to stay together. The UN Guidance provides that planned relocation should “maintain social cohesion and kinship ties.” A massage therapist, 44, said an official became angry when she posed questions about the suitability of the relocation site: “The engineer pointed at me and said they studied engineering and would not risk their licenses over the project [if it weren’t suitable].” Community members said that in response to their concerns, local authorities told them the site would be raised to the same height as the road dike to protect them from flooding. However, the embankment works never reached that elevation, and the site remains below the dike. One engineer who worked on the relocation said that the road dike design does not allow raising the site to the same level. Human Rights Watch visited the relocation site from July 12 to 14, at the beginning of the rainy season, when at high tide the floodwater was knee- to thigh-deep. Human Rights Watch observed children wading through floodwaters, and older people who could not leave their homes while they were flooded. Residents, who described similar flooding year-round, needed to wade through flooded areas to reach the dike road. Click to expand Image The main street at the site where the Pulo Island community has been relocated lies 1.9 meters below the dike road. On the day Human Rights Watch visited, when there was light rain, the street was flooded 20 centimeters deep. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development, which would normally have been involved in the relocation project, told Human Rights Watch that, pending further on-site assessments, the “reported physical characteristics of the site raise concerns regarding its suitability for permanent housing.” The Philippines is obligated under international human rights law to respect, protect, and fulfill everyone’s economic, social, and cultural rights. This includes protecting people from reasonably foreseeable climate change risks, including flooding and other impacts. The relocation of Pulo Island residents was inconsistent with international standards as reflected in the UN Guidance. The Commission on Human Rights told Human Rights Watch that had the project been referred to them, they could have helped ensure that rights-based processes were followed. The commission also said it will conduct a fact-finding investigation into the matter. “Communities in the Philippines living in flood-prone areas are already facing the consequences of climate change and shouldn’t have to suffer further from botched government relocations,” Buan said. “Donors supporting the Philippine response to the effects of climate change should press the government to ensure that every aspect of relocation meets international human rights standards.” For more details and accounts about the planned relocation in Pampanga, please see below. Relocation from Pulo Click to expand Image Satellite imagery showing the progressive removal of Pulo Island beginning in 2021 through dredging by the Department of Public Works and Highways. Images © 2026 US NARA, Airbus, Vantor, Google Earth. Analysis and graphics © 2026 Human Rights Watch Few owned the land on which their houses stood, but many were farmer tenants or “share tenants,” for whom the landowner provides the capital and the tenant provides labor, and both share in the harvest. Residents did not pay rent, but they paid the property tax that the local government collected annually on residential lands. Under the Philippine Right-of-Way Act, those without legal claims on the land are still entitled to compensation for their structures. Macabebe is part of the Pampanga Delta, the portion of Pampanga, Bulacan, and Bataan provinces composed of low swampy lands prone to flooding. In the early 1990s, the Japan International Cooperation Agency funded the Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase I (PDDP I/Delta I), under which 1,851 households were to be resettled, but the project was never completed. The Pulo Island residents opposed being relocated by the project and remained. Two engineers from the flood control cluster of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), Tomas Edison Olalia and Alvin Diaz, told Human Rights Watch that the removal of the island was “already long overdue” because it had been proposed under the earlier project. Since 2011, the Philippine government has spent Php 1.93 trillion (US$30 billion) on flood control projects across the country through the department. Almost one third, or Php 545 billion ($8.7 billion), was spent between July 2022 and May 2025, during the administration of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., amid allegations of massive corruption in flood control projects. At least 45 public officials have been charged in the anti-graft court in connection with various flood-control projects, most of them DPWH officials.The officials interviewed have not been implicated, nor did Human Rights Watch investigate corruption in the Pulo Island project. In 2019 and 2020, the department’s flood control cluster awarded two contracts worth Php 157 million ($2.6 million) to remove Pulo Island through its yearly flood mitigation program, according to contracts and budget line items. DPWH officials told Human Rights Watch that the project was initiated by then-Mayor Balgan. In separate letters sent by the former mayor to the agency and the agency to the residents, the community was termed “informal settler families” who needed to be removed from a “danger zone.” Under Philippine law, informal settler families occupy land without consent, or live in places considered “danger areas.” Olalia and Diaz, the engineers involved in the project, said Balgan requested the island’s dredging under a 2017 policy that instructs local government to “immediately commence the removal of illegal structures in all danger areas,” and communicated directly with now retired DPWH project manager Isabelita Manalo. Danger areas included “river banks, shorelines, creeks, waterways, esteros (estuaries) ... which when occupied for residential purposes actually pose danger to the life, safety and property of either the concerned residents, or of the general community.” Other Philippine agencies were not involved in the project, based on interviews with officials and written responses sent to Human Rights Watch by the Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development and the Commmission on Human Rights. “This was an isolated case,” said Olalia, referring to the lack of involvement by other government departments. “We just responded to the request of the LGU [local government unit] because it had a valid reason; the island was in a danger zone.” The Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development is normally the lead agency for planned relocation, along with the National Housing Authority, which are responsible under the National Resettlement Policy to check the feasibility of the relocation site and can provide financing for new houses. When informal settlers are affected by a resettlement, the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor should monitor the situation, according to the Department of Interior and Local Government’s resettlement guidelines. The Commission on Human Rights also has an oversight role in such cases, as its internal rules require the agency to “ensure strict compliance to the Commission on Human Rights Advisory on the Right to Adequate Housing and Humane Treatment of Informal Settlers.” In addition, the interior department’s resettlement guidelines require oversight by a local inter-agency committee or a local housing board. Human Rights Watch sent right of reply letters outlining the findings on September 21 and received responses from the human settlements department and the Commission on Human Rights. The DPWH, the municipal office in Macabebe, and the Presidential Commission on Urban Poor did not reply. “There was no check and balance,” said Ferdinand Zambrano, the project development officer at the local Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development office. The current mayor, Leonardo Flores, is Mayor Balgan’s brother. Flores’ office referred Human Rights Watch to Jomel Cruz, the disaster risk reduction officer, who was the municipal administrator during that time. Cruz said that there are no documents pertaining to the project among the files turned over by the former administration. The relocation site may be further affected by the planned Pampanga Delta Development Project Phase II (PDDP II or Delta II), which is undergoing feasibility studies, according to plans seen by Human Rights Watch that show Macabebe within the PDDP II project area. Key Human Rights Issues Relating to Planned Relocation Click to expand Image Graphic © 2026 Human Rights Watch International human rights law on planned relocations derives from various human rights treaties that the Philippines has ratified, notably the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights. It is also reflected in international standards and guidance, such as the UN Guidance on Planned Relocation and the UN special rapporteur on internally displaced persons Report on Planned Relocation, to help governments plan and carry out relocations of communities at risk in a rights-respecting manner. Consultation Under international human rights law, planned relocation and other government action that directly affects protected economic and social rights—particularly housing, land, relocation, eviction, water, or livelihoods—needs to be preceded by meaningful, informed, and participatory consultation with affected communities as an important procedural safeguard. Such consultation requires timely and accessible information, an opportunity to express views, and genuine consideration of those views. UN guidance and human rights standards establish that national and local governments need to ensure that planned relocation is a measure of last resort, and ensure that affected communities are meaningfully involved in decisions about a potential move. The UN Guidance says there needs to be some “flexibility to accommodate persons who may choose not to participate in the relocation,” and an opportunity for affected residents “to propose alternative options.” All members of the relocated community interviewed by Human Rights Watch said their concerns and questions about relocation were not given due consideration. What happened was not consultation but an “imposition,” said an 81-year-old woman. During meetings held by officials, including in the local language, residents said their opposition was merely noted. “They simply gave out forms for us to sign and promised us a relocation,” said Jenny Datu, 50. DPWH officials acknowledged that their staff did not conduct detailed consultations with residents, saying that their role was limited to technical assistance on the project. Pulo Island’s former residents said they ultimately agreed to move because officials said they could have a relocation site that would allow the community to stay together. In 2021, residents received “Agreement to Demolish and Remove Improvements” forms that were in English, which is not their preferred language. Some residents said they were frustrated that they received no assistance from anyone, such as a lawyer, to discuss the form. “We had no choice,” said Mary Grace Liguid, 38. “People just arrived measuring our houses, our lands. We had no choice but to agree, because you can’t be left there.” Right to Information The right to receive information, set out in article 19(2) of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, is a core component of a human rights-based approach to planned relocation. Information should be provided in a clear and accessible manner, and should include anticipated disaster and climate risks as well as the social, physical, and economic impacts of the relocation. The UN Guidance provides that adequate, advanced, up-to-date, and accessible information on the rationale for relocation, as well as alternatives considered, is essential to minimize the risk of forced evictions. Residents said they were told various reasons for their removal from the island, including that the island was blocking the flow of the river, which is the reason stated in government documents. Community members also said they were told the island was shaped like a cone, being eroded from underneath, and could collapse at any time. “They scared us that our island was running out of soil, and we will be washed away,” said a 46-year-old man. Olalia and Diaz said this information about the island being eroded did not come from their office. The current municipal engineer of Macabebe said the local government would have no capacity to come up with such an assessment. Satellite imagery analysis by Human Rights Watch shows that, in the 36 years preceding their removal, the surface area of the island reduced by 5.2 percent, from 25 hectares in 1984 to 23.7 hectares in 2020. Relocated residents said they could not recall being given the opportunity to discuss any risk assessment with government officials. None could recall any discussion about ways they could stay on the island. A lack of information and community concerns about compensation also caused delays, as documented by DPWH itself. “Unless the people paid for the houses to be demolished, they will not transfer to the designated relocation site,” said a 2021 department order, rescheduling that phase of the dredging, which was only completed between 2022 and 2023. The payment arrangement left residents with no choice but to demolish their homes. Once they signed the demolition forms, they could receive 70 percent of the assessed value by traveling to Metro Manila to cash their compensation check. They were expected to immediately demolish their homes upon receiving the partial payment and would only receive the remaining 30 percent after providing photos and videos of their demolished homes. Most of the residents interviewed said they felt rushed to demolish their homes and cited rumors of allocated funds running out. “We were panicking,” said Esmeralda Tubig, a 46-year-old daycare teacher. “First of all, you’d demolish your house without complete payment, then you have your daily life to think about. We didn’t know where we’d get our livelihood, then suddenly we also did not know where we’d live.” More than a dozen residents said they also felt intimidated by local officials. “It was raining heavily that time, and they wanted us to start demolishing our houses,” said a 61-year-old construction worker. Residents said that they never received other forms of compensation, including for their crops. The UN Guidance states that people should “have the right to equitable compensation for their land and any other relinquished assets related to that land.” One resident burned their own trees to turn them into charcoal to at least earn some money before moving. The Philippine National Resettlement Policy Framework states that relocated people should be given a pathway to secure land tenure in their resettlement site, whether through leasehold or the right to use other property or another contractual arrangement. A 33-year-old man said he remembered discussing with authorities whether they would receive land titles at the relocation site. “Because if we don’t have titles, we’re squatters here,” he said. Suitability and Standard of Living at the New Site The national and local governments are responsible for ensuring an adequate standard of living at relocation sites. The UN Guidance says that in relocating a community, the government must “provide the necessary conditions [for them] to build a sustainable life of dignity in their place of settlement.” The National Resettlement Policy Framework also states that “resettlement sites should not be located in areas with exposure to natural hazards” such as “low-lying and flood-prone areas.” Human Rights Watch, on August 5, visited the relocation site and measured that the main street was flooded to a depth of 20 centimeters. Using a smartphone scan, the researcher then processed the images with photogrammetry to determine that the elevation difference between the top of the floodwater and the road dike was about 1.7 meters. Human Rights Watch found that the main street of the relocation site was built about 1.9 meters below the dike. Residents said that the site floods to the same level frequently throughout the year during high water levels in the Pampanga River, even during the hot dry season, from March to May. They must wade through flooded streets to reach the road dike year round but more often simply stay in their houses. Officials involved in the relocation had promised that the former fishpond would, after embankment works, match the height of the road dike beside it, several people said. The engineers said they made no such promise and had no role in selecting the relocation site, although one of their contractors did some embankment work on the site to reassure the community. The residents said that when they began moving to the site in 2022, work was ongoing to raise the site. “The site was unfinished when we moved,” said Ely Barsana, a 44-year-old massage therapist. “It was half-baked.” The work stopped eventually, with no update from authorities. Representatives from the municipal office in Macabebe said they had limited knowledge of the project. Families decided to start building their houses because their compensation money was better spent on their new home instead of on rent. “How can we wait longer?” said a 58-year-old woman. “We already demolished our house. We were renting. The payment on our house would run out the longer we rent.” Some residents were able to afford to elevate their houses, but many others could not. The authorities did not warn them that their relocation site could flood. Maria Mallari, 50, lives in a bungalow that she says is rarely dry. Her furniture is damaged, and she lifts heavy appliances every day to protect them from water. When the water subsides, the family scrubs the floor clean, only for it to be flooded again the next day. “I’m sick of it, so sick of it,” she said. Residents said they had fewer options for livelihood now. Several of them relied on selling fruit and vegetables they grew on the island to supplement their irregular incomes as laborers, construction workers, tricycle drivers, farmers, and fisherfolk. Some residents have left their families in the relocation site to seek work elsewhere. Although the relocation site is closer to the town center, frequent flooding requires a longer journey to access services like the hospital than when the community lived on Pulo Island. In July, a woman fell ill but could not be immediately transported to the hospital because the water level was too high, making boat transfer risky. She was in critical condition in the hospital for weeks, but has since recovered. Children have to wade through flood to get to and from school every day.

items.title: Parlement : organisation d’un atelier destiné à renforcer le rôle des députés dans le suivi des politiques relatives à l’immigration et aux réfugiés
items.description: L'Assemblée nationale mauritanienne a lancé ce lundi un atelier parlementaire consacré au renforcement du rôle des députés dans le suivi et l'évaluation des politiques publiques relatives à l'immigration et aux réfugiés. Selon l’Assemblée, cet atelier vise notamment à renforcer les capacités des parlementaires dans les domaines de la législation, du contrôle de l’action gouvernementale et du suivi de la « Stratégie nationale de gestion des migrations » (SNGM), à redynamiser la commission parlementaire chargée des questions d’immigration et de réfugiés, présidée par le député Zeine El-Abidine Ould El-Mounir Ould Tolba. Les travaux de l’atelier ont donné lieu à des exposés et à des débats portant sur la compréhension de la Stratégie nationale de gestion des migrations, notamment ses orientations, son cadre institutionnel et juridique, ses mécanismes de coordination, la gestion des flux migratoires, la protection des migrants et des réfugiés, ainsi que les liens entre migration, emploi et développement.

items.title: Man City bananas ‘brought fun back’, says Varadi
items.description: Former Manchester City striker Imre Varadi said it was “brilliant to see” the club’s fans waving inflatable bananas at Anfield on Sunday and feels it “brought a lot of fun back”. Varadi was nicknamed ‘Imre Banana’ by City fans during his two-year spell with the club in the late 1980s and they began taking inflatable bananas to games when they played in the old Second Division. The craze continued into the early 90s, with City fans taking bananas to games intermittently since, and dozens re-emerged at Sunday’s game. City’s 3-0 win over Liverpool was the club’s first game since being found guilty of 114 charges related to breaches of Premier League financial rules between 2009-10 and 2017-18. With the club facing sanctions such as a points deduction or expulsion from the Premier League, City fans took bananas to Anfield as a nod to their yo-yo years in the 1980s. Varadi, who now sells inflatable bananas via the club and whose X account is @imre_banana, told BBC Radio 5 Live Drive: “It was amazing, [it’s] bringing a lot of fun back into the game. “The game itself was a terrific game obviously but just to see the inflatable craze coming back from the 80s when I was playing at the old Maine Road, it was a joy.” Varadi joined City from West Brom in October 1986 and scored 26 goals in 65 appearances before moving to Sheffield Wednesday in September 1988. “Somebody started to call me Imre Banana and then, the following game, there were 10, 20, 25 bananas and then it just grew and grew and grew until every football club had an inflatable,” he added. “I started it, but it was 40 years ago, and it’s still going strong now, as we all saw at Anfield. I’m really proud of it. “It’s bringing a lot of joy to the game. It’s great to see.”

items.title: Nouakchott : montée en flèche des prix des tomates atteignant désormais 3500 ouguiyas
items.description: Les marchés de légumes de Nouakchott connaissent une pénurie de tomates, dont le prix a atteint 3 500 ouguiyas le kilo au marché marocain, dans le centre de la capitale, comme l'a constaté le correspondant de Sahara Media lors d'une visite sur place. Les commerçants ont évoqué une crise d'approvisionnement en tomates qui a débuté hier. L’un des commerçants a déclaré que les tomates se faisaient rares et que les quantités restantes se vendaient jusqu’à 3 500 MRO le kilo. Il a ajouté que les tomates figuraient parmi les principaux légumes du marché et que cette pénurie signifiait l’existence d’une crise pour ce produit, susceptible de se répercuter sur les prix si la rareté de l’offre persistait. Le correspondant de Sahara Media a constaté, lors de sa tournée, la rareté des tomates sur le marché, tandis que les commerçants ont évoqué la difficulté à s’en procurer depuis hier, dans un contexte de craintes quant à la persistance de la crise et à son impact sur les prix.

items.title: Mauritanie-Allemagne : la coopération dans le domaine de la santé militaire évoquée lors d’une réunion à Nouakchott
items.description: La Direction générale des services de santé des forces armées et des forces de sécurité de Mauritanie a examiné ce lundi, avec une délégation militaire allemande, les moyens de coopérer et d'échanger des expériences dans le domaine de la santé militaire. L'armée mauritanienne a indiqué, dans un message publié sur sa page Facebook officielle, que le directeur général de la Direction, le colonel pharmacien Mohamed Mahmoud Taleb Jidou, avait reçu la délégation allemande, conduite par le lieutenant-colonel Friedel, au siège de la Direction. Elle a ajouté que la délégation avait assisté à une présentation sur les missions et l'organisation de la Direction, ainsi que sur son rôle dans la fourniture d'un soutien sanitaire aux forces armées et aux forces de sécurité.

items.title: Daily Insight for CEOs: The CEO as Chief Decision Maker
items.description: By Ernest De-Graft Egyir Insight. Decision-making is one of the CEO’s most important responsibilities. Every major decision about strategy, people, investment, operations, and risk influences the organization’s direction and performance. Effective CEOs do not attempt to make every decision themselves. They establish clear decision-making principles, involve the right people, distinguish urgent matters from important ones, and ensure that critical decisions are made at the appropriate level. Key Strategies: Establish clear principles for making strategic and operational decisions. Distinguish decisions that require CEO involvement from those that can be delegated. Use reliable data, professional judgment, and relevant stakeholder perspectives. Assess the risks and long-term implications of major decisions. Review the outcomes of significant decisions and apply the lessons learned. CEO Leadership Actions. Identify the decisions that require your direct attention this week. Clarify decision-making authority across the executive team. Review whether previous major decisions have delivered their intended results. Actionable Tip. Before making a major decision, ask: “Does this decision advance our strategy, create sustainable value, and position the organization for future success?” Why This Matters? The quality of an organization’s decisions shapes its performance, resilience, and competitive position. When the CEO establishes a disciplined decision-making culture, the organization can act with greater confidence, speed, and accountability. About the Author. Ernest De-Graft Egyir, CEO advisor, Thought Leader and Founding CEO of Chief Executives Network Ghana, convenes the Ghana CEO Summit and served on Ghana’s Economic Dialogue Planning Committee

items.title: Le ministre des affaires étrangères : de nombreuses réformes ont renforcé les liens entre les Mauritaniens de l’étranger et leur pays d’origine
items.description: Le ministre mauritanien des Affaires étrangères, de la coopération africaine et des mauritaniens de l’extérieur Mohamed Salem Merzoug, a déclaré que le gouvernement avait mis en œuvre plusieurs réformes qui ont renforcé les liens entre les Mauritaniens de l'étranger et leur pays d'origine. Le ministre s'exprimait alors qu'il présidait une réunion par visioconférence avec les chefs des missions diplomatiques et consulaires, dans le cadre des préparatifs en cours pour l'organisation de la première édition du Forum des communautés mauritaniennes à l'étranger, qui se tiendra à Nouakchott les 29, 30 et 31 octobre courant. Le ministre a évoqué « une série de réformes et de mesures visant à renforcer le lien entre les citoyens de l’étranger et leur patrie, parmi lesquelles figurent notamment la restructuration du secteur des affaires étrangères et l’intégration des Mauritaniens de l’étranger dans sa dénomination officielle, ainsi que la révision de la loi sur la nationalité afin de permettre aux citoyens détenant une nationalité étrangère de conserver leur nationalité mauritanienne ». Il a également souligné « le renforcement de la représentation politique des communautés en leur permettant d’élire des députés qui les représentent directement à l’Assemblée nationale, ainsi que la mise à disposition des services d’état civil et des services consulaires via l’application « Houwiti » et la plateforme de services consulaires numériques ». Il a déclaré que le Forum des communautés mauritaniennes à l’étranger « représente une occasion de faire évoluer la relation avec les communautés mauritaniennes à l’étranger, passant d’une communication ponctuelle à un partenariat institutionnel durable, et d’un traitement au cas par cas des revendications à l’élaboration d’une politique nationale intégrée à l’égard des Mauritaniens à l’étranger ». Le ministre a appelé « à profiter de l’occasion offerte par le forum pour organiser des opérations de recensement à grande échelle des communautés, des compétences et des associations, afin de contribuer à la constitution d’une base de données nationale facilitant la planification, l’amélioration des services et l’orientation des politiques publiques ». Il a souligné « le rôle central que jouent les missions diplomatiques et consulaires dans la communication avec les citoyens mauritaniens résidant à l’étranger, la protection de leurs intérêts, la mise à disposition de services à leur proximité et le renforcement de leurs liens avec la patrie ».

items.title: JEPPC 2026 : L’université Joseph Ki-Zerbo remporte la 3ᵉ édition de la Coupe de la citoyenneté
items.description: L’Université Joseph Ki-Zerbo (UJKZ) a remporté la troisième édition de la Coupe de la Citoyenneté face à l’Université de l’Unité africaine, ce 12 octobre 2026 à Ouagadougou. Au terme des deux périodes de 30 minutes, les deux équipes n’ont pas réussi à se départager. Le gardien de l’UJKZ a finalement offert le trophée à son équipe en arrêtant le dernier tir adverse lors de la séance des tirs au but. La finale s’est déroulée en présence du ministre de la Justice, Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala, et du ministre délégué chargé des Ressources animales et halieutiques, Amadou Dicko. Malgré la domination de l’UJKZ pendant le temps réglementaire, la victoire s’est jouée aux tirs au but. La rencontre s’est disputée dans un esprit de fair-play, avec un seul carton jaune distribué, un comportement salué par le ministre de la Justice. Organisée dans le cadre de la deuxième phase des Journées nationales d’engagement patriotique et de participation citoyenne (JEPPC) 2026, cette compétition s’inscrit sous le thème « Tous pour le Made in Burkina : faisons de chaque achat un acte de souveraineté » . Elle vise notamment à promouvoir les valeurs citoyennes et à renforcer la cohésion entre les jeunes. Le football constitue un cadre d’apprentissage de la discipline, du respect des règles et de l’esprit d’équipe, seon Me Edasso Rodrigue Bayala . « Sur un terrain de football comme dans la société, nul ne peut gagner durablement sans respecter les règles, accepter la décision de l’arbitre et reconnaître la valeur de l’adversaire » , a-t-il souligné. Le ministre a également rappelé que la compétition avait réuni 16 équipes issues d’écoles de formation professionnelle, d’universités et d’organisations de la société civile. Au total, 16 matchs ont été disputés, dont 12 lors de la première phase et quatre pendant la seconde. Il a exprimé le souhait de voir cette initiative prendre de l’ampleur et s’étendre davantage sur le territoire national. Du côté des vainqueurs, la satisfaction était au rendez-vous. Le capitaine de l’Université Joseph Ki-Zerbo, Mikail Natayin, s’est réjoui de ce succès après une précédente finale perdue. Il a salué l’accompagnement des encadreurs et félicité les organisateurs pour cette compétition qui, selon lui, favorise la cohésion et les échanges entre jeunes. La troisième édition de la Coupe de la Citoyenneté s’achève ainsi sur la victoire de l’UJKZ, mais aussi sur un appel au respect des règles, à la solidarité et à l’engagement collectif, des valeurs que les organisateurs souhaitent voir se prolonger au-delà du terrain. Josué TIENDREBEOGO Faso7 L’article JEPPC 2026 : L’université Joseph Ki-Zerbo remporte la 3ᵉ édition de la Coupe de la citoyenneté est apparu en premier sur Faso7 .

items.title: Gouvernance locale : Une formation pour consolider le rôle des organisations de veille citoyenne à Loumbila
items.description: Les acteurs de la veille citoyenne de la commune de Loumbila ont entamé, ce lundi 12 octobre 2026, une session de formation consacrée au contrôle citoyen. Prévue pour durer deux jours, cette initiative vise à renforcer les capacités des organisations locales afin de leur permettre de mieux jouer leur rôle dans la gouvernance communale et le développement local. Initiée par le Laboratoire Citoyennetés, en partenariat avec Solidar Suisse, cette session de formation se tient les 12 et 13 octobre 2026. Elle entend familiariser les organisations de veille citoyenne et les acteurs clés de la commune avec les notions et concepts du contrôle citoyen, les outiller sur ses enjeux et améliorer leurs démarches sur le terrain. Quelques participants à la formation. Au cours de la formation, les participants vont échanger notamment sur les différentes notions liées à la veille citoyenne, les mécanismes du contrôle citoyen et la mobilisation des ressources nécessaires à la conduite de leurs activités. Les discussions porteront également sur les moyens de renforcer la mobilisation communautaire, dans un contexte où les questions de sécurité nationale et de défense des intérêts du pays occupent une place importante. Les principaux bénéficiaires sont les membres de la Coordination nationale des associations de veille citoyenne (CNAVC), qui exercent déjà des activités de veille au niveau local. L'objectif est de consolider leurs acquis et de les accompagner afin qu'ils puissent contribuer davantage à la bonne marche des communes et au développement communautaire. Bie Thiono, chargé de programme au Laboratoire Citoyenneté La session a réuni une quinzaine de participants, issus notamment de la CNAVC, d'Organisations de la société civile (OSC), de radios locales et de la mairie. Cette diversité doit favoriser le partage d'expériences et la concertation entre les différents acteurs engagés dans la vie communale. Pour le chargé de programme au Laboratoire Citoyennetés, Bie Thiono, cette initiative répond à un besoin exprimé par des membres de la CNAVC, désireux de mieux comprendre leur rôle et de renforcer leur contribution à la gouvernance locale. « Nous avons été approchés par certains membres de la CNAVC, pour exprimer le besoin d'avoir des connaissances sur leur rôle, surtout de veiller à jouer pleinement leur rôle. C'est ainsi que nous avons jugé bon de les accompagner à travers cette formation », a-t-il expliqué. À l'issue de la formation, les organisateurs attendent des structures participantes qu'elles assument pleinement leur rôle de veille, contribuent à l'amélioration de la gouvernance locale et accompagnent les autorités communales dans l'accomplissement de leurs missions au service des populations. Seyba Compaoré, président de la délégation spéciale de la commune de Loumbila. Dans son mot, le président de la délégation spéciale de la commune de Loumbila, Seyba Compaoré, s'est réjoui de cette formation qui va profiter aux acteurs de la veille citoyenne. « Les structures de veille citoyenne sont des démembrements de la commune. Ce sont des acteurs de développement de la commune. Pour nous, tout acteur qui reçoit une formation va certainement contribuer au développement de la commune », a-t-il expliqué. Il a par ailleurs souhaité que les acteurs qui reçoivent la formation fassent bon usage des connaissances qu'ils auront acquises. Le chargé de mission à la présidence du Faso pour la région d'Oubri, Boureima Sawadogo, a remercié le Laboratoire Citoyennetés pour la formation. Selon lui, les acteurs ont besoin de connaissances supplémentaires pour être davantage utiles dans leurs différentes localités. « Nos acteurs ont vraiment besoin de connaissances. Je pense que cette formation est la bienvenue. Ça va nous aider dans nos actions. Ça va nous aider également dans nos différentes localités, pour qu'on puisse être plus utiles qu'avant », a-t-il souligné. Boureima Sawadogo, chargé de mission à la présidence du Faso pour la région d'Oubri. Jean Élysée Nikiéma Lefaso.net

items.title: Burnham had formal meeting with Man City chair while mayor
items.description: Prime Minister Andy Burnham had one formal meeting with Manchester City chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak while mayor of Greater Manchester, according to the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. A GMCA statement said the meeting took place in October 2021 at the UK Government’s Global Investment Summit, arranged by the Department for International Trade. He also met Al Mubarak informally in the stands at a City home fixture in September 2019, when attending Vincent Kompany’s testimonial as a guest of the club. Burnham said on Sunday he would release details of his meetings with senior figures at Manchester City. It follows criticism of his comments in the wake of the club being found guilty of all charges related to breaches of the Premier League’s financial rules. A GMCA spokesperson said Burnham had been a guest at City home matches on a “small number of occasions” and that the hospitality had been “declared in the usual way”. The GMCA also said representatives of Greater Manchester sporting clubs would “routinely join business delegations” on international visits during Burnham’s time as mayor. It noted this included Manchester United representatives travelling to Austin and Dublin, Lancashire County Cricket Club joining a delegation to India, and City staff supporting visits to China and Japan. Shadow sports minister Louie French said that Burnham “cannot hide behind the GMCA” and “must take responsibility for this himself” and urged him to “come clean about his relationship with City Football Group”. “This is far from the full transparency that football fans deserve,” French said. “We have been given precious little information about these meetings, what was discussed and what may have been agreed. If Burnham has nothing to hide, why is he being so tight-lipped? “His bizarre intervention in defence of Man City’s owners has raised serious concerns among fans.” An independent commission found City had broken rules over a nine-year period between 2009 and 2018 by creating “sham” contracts with commercial partners to secretly funnel more than £830m into their football operations. Burnham’s previous role as mayor of Greater Manchester has raised questions about his relationship with City’s Abu Dhabi ownership, with Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch demanding that No 10 release all details of meetings between the prime minister and senior figures at the club. “I’ve been asked by the leader of the opposition to publish details of my meetings, which I’m happy to do, and I’m going to,” Burnham told the Rest is Politics podcast. “I will quite clearly put out there everything that I have done working with them in my previous role as Mayor of Greater Manchester. “None of it is recent, actually, in terms of the meetings I had. I only had one significant meeting, actually, and that was in 2021.” The prime minister initially told the BBC he would be “really concerned” if Manchester City’s owners decided to sell up following the guilty verdict, before later denying that his reaction had “downplayed the seriousness of the findings”. However, some Premier League clubs were so “astonished” by Burnham’s stance that, according to sources, they were “concerned” about political interference in the appeal process. Sanctions are yet to be announced, and City have lodged an appeal against the verdict. City returned to action for the first time since the guilty verdict when they played at Liverpool on Sunday, winning 3-0 . Burnham defends comments on Man City Burnham was mayor of Manchester from 2017 until earlier this year and his tenure took place during a sustained period of success for City. As mayor, he championed investment from the Gulf as a way of growing Manchester’s economy, a strategy which was initially pursued by the city’s leaders before Burnham became the inaugural elected mayor of the Greater Manchester Combined Authority. “I don’t think I misspoke,” said Burnham of his past comments on Manchester City’s owners. “What I would say is my mind hadn’t been on all of the issues. My mind had been on Labour Party conference and I was doing interviews in relation to it. “And also, I didn’t link those two things. You know, the questions linked those two things. What I would say is they’re very separate. “The football issues are different from the investment issues. People will try and conflate those two things, but they shouldn’t, in my view. “The football issues, the findings of the independent commission are serious, as I said in the interview.” The entire process involving the charges against Manchester City is independent of the Premier League. An independent commission held a 42-day hearing in 2024 which led to the verdict announced last month, with City also guilty of all charges except one relating to non-cooperation with the Premier League investigation. The commission’s report said that “a number of important club witnesses gave false evidence in key respects and that some knowingly gave untrue and dishonest evidence”. A separate independent appeal board will hear City’s appeal. The club continues to deny any wrongdoing.

items.title: Is Ghana producing too many lawyers? What is the best lawyer-to-citizen ratio?
items.description: By Richard Nii Amarh, ESQ On Friday, October 9, 2026, the General Legal Council of Ghana recorded the names of 1,568 individuals onto the roll of lawyers, marking the single largest number of individuals called to the bar since Ghana started training its own lawyers. The prestigious flaunting of photos by the new lawyers, alongside their families and friends, has re-ignited an annual conversation. Many are asking whether Ghana is producing too many lawyers and if our economy can absorb them into meaningful jobs. Concerned commentators often compare the number of lawyers to engineers, doctors, and other professionals, questioning which field is most critical for national development. Others worry about the heavy representation of lawyers in politics, which feeds into the persistent—though statistically unfair—perception that both lawyers and politicians are trained to bend the truth. This article explores and compares the lawyer-to-citizen ratios of various countries near and far, examines the diverse career paths available to lawyers, and sets the stage for an informed conclusion on whether Ghana’s legal boom is a blessing or a burden. A Global Perspective: Lawyer-to-Citizen Ratios 1. The United Kingdom (UK) Population: ~70 million Lawyer Population: ~217,000 Ratio: 1 lawyer to every 440 citizens GDP: ~$3.4 trillion Average Income: £60,000 ($80,000 USD) per year 2. The United States of America (USA) Population: ~350 million Lawyer Population: ~1,374,720 Ratio: 1 lawyer to every 240 citizens (one of the highest densities globally) GDP: ~$32.5 trillion Average Income: ~$170,000 USD per year 3. China Population: ~1.4 billion Lawyer Population: ~830,000 Ratio: 1 lawyer to every 1,700 citizens GDP: ~$18 trillion Average Income: ¥900,000 ($140,000 USD) per year 4. Nigeria Population: ~242 million Lawyer Population: ~225,000 Ratio: 1 lawyer to every 2,000 citizens GDP: ~$290 billion Average Income: ₦14 million ($10,000 USD) per year 5. West African Neighbors (Nigeria Excluded) Benin: Population of 14 million | GDP: $24.4 billion | 500 active lawyers | Ratio: ~1:32,000 | Average Salary: ~7 million CFA ($13,000 USD). Togo: Population of 8.6 million | GDP: $11.9 billion | 350 active lawyers | Ratio: ~1:30,000 | Average Salary: 2M–5M CFA ($3,300 to $8,300 USD). Ivory Coast: Population of 32 million | GDP: $99.7 billion | 800 active lawyers | Ratio: ~1:40,000 to 1:50,000 | Average Salary: 2.4M–6.7M CFA ($4,000 to $11,000 USD). Burkina Faso: Population of 23–24 million | GDP: ~$32.5 billion | ~300–400 lawyers | Ratio: ~1:65,000 to 1:75,000 | Average Salary: 2.4M–5.5M CFA ($4,000 to $9,000 USD). Liberia: Population of ~5.5–6 million | GDP: ~$5.2 billion | ~600–900 lawyers | Ratio: ~1:7,000 to 1:9,000 | Average Salary: $4,000 to $12,000 USD. 6. Ghana Population: ~35 million GDP: $77 billion Lawyer Population: Nearly 10,000 (according to Ghana Bar Association data) Ratio: 1 lawyer to every 4,000 citizens Average Income: Estimated at GHS 180,000 annually (~$15,000 USD) The Local Reality: Courts, Judges, and Concentration Legal services are tightly tethered to economic activity. Unsurprisingly, the vast majority of lawyers in Ghana are heavily concentrated in Accra, Kumasi, and Takoradi, leaving other regions and secondary cities underserved. While hard scientific research on whether Ghana has an “excess” of lawyers is sparse, a few critical metrics helps clarify the picture: Ghana currently has roughly 500 courts operating nationwide. The Judicial Service Staff Association recently reported that there are about 130 courts without judges (currently only qualified lawyers can be appointed to the bench). The bottleneck here isn’t a shortage of lawyers willing to serve as judges; rather, it is a matter of financial clearance. Just like any other public sector employment, the Ministry of Finance must approve funding before judges can be appointed and paid. The absence of judges in these 130 courts puts enormous pressure on the justice system, causing endless adjournments, delayed adjudications, and intense frustration for litigants. If Ghana is struggling to fund 130 more judges, why are we pumping 1,500 new lawyers onto the market every year? Beyond Litigation: Where Do Lawyers Work? A law degree is remarkably versatile. Beyond traditional courtroom battles, new lawyers enter a wide range of rewarding career paths: Litigation Counsel: Representing individual, corporate, or institutional clients across all court levels (Circuit, High Court, Supreme Court) in civil, criminal, land, and human rights disputes. Corporate & Commercial Practice: Advising businesses on corporate governance, mergers and acquisitions, regulatory compliance, and foreign investments. Intellectual Property (IP) Practice: Managing trademark, copyright, and patent registrations, alongside IP licensing and disputes. In-House Counsel / Legal Officer: Managing legal risks, drafting commercial contracts, and ensuring compliance for banks, telcos, mining firms, and fintechs. Company Secretary: Serving as principal administrative and governance officer for corporate boards under the Companies Act. State Attorney / Legal Counsel: Working within the Attorney-General’s Department and Ministry of Justice to advise government bodies, prosecute state cases, and draft legislation. Judicial Service: Serving as Magistrates, Registrars, or judicial research assistants. Regulatory Bodies & Commissions: Enforcing sector-specific laws at institutions like the Bank of Ghana, SEC, NCA, and EPA. Arbitrator or Mediator: Specializing in out-of-court settlements under Ghana’s Alternative Dispute Resolution framework. Law Lecturer / Researcher: Teaching and training future advocates at faculties like UG, KNUST, GIMPA, UPSA, and the Ghana School of Law. Advocacy & Policy Consultant: Driving public interest litigation, law reform, and human rights work with think tanks and NGOs. Conclusion: Are We Producing Too Many? To answer whether Ghana is producing too many lawyers, I will give a typical lawyer’s answer: It depends. Major Western economies can comfortably support large numbers of lawyers and sustain high-income jobs despite low lawyer-to-citizen ratios, largely due to the sheer size of their markets. In West Africa, however, Nigeria stands out as the only country with a lower lawyer-to-citizen ratio than Ghana—and it possesses a significantly larger economy. If Ghana rapidly scales up its economic power to match the growing influx of annual law graduates, these numbers won’t pose a problem. However, if economic growth remains stagnant, policymakers will inevitably need to take a hard look at the trajectory and regulation of legal education in Ghana. Disclaimer: Most statistics used in this article were compiled from online sources and actual figures are subject to minor variations. items.title: FRSC ​‌‍‍‍‍⁠⁠‍​‍​⁠​‌​⁠‌​confirms female NYSC member dead in Ibadan auto crash
items.description: The Federal Road Safety Corps (FRSC), Oyo Sector Command, has confirmed the death of a female corps member in a road crash on Monday in Ibadan. The Sector Commander in Oyo State, Corps Commander Kehinde Dahunsi, disclosed this in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN). Dahunsi said that the crash involved a motorcycle and an articulated truck. According to him, the female corps member lost her life in the accident while the motorcycle rider sustained a fracture in his leg. He said that while the body of the corps member had been deposited at the State Hospital morgue, the motorcyclist was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan, for medical attention. The sector commander noted that details of the late corps member could not be ascertained at the time of the rescue operation. “We recorded a traffic crash today around Agodi Gardens within the Ibadan metropolis. It involved a truck and a motorcycle carrying a corps member. “Unfortunately, we lost the corps member, and the rider also sustained a fracture in his leg. “We carried out emergency rescue operations; we conveyed the body of the late corps member to the State Hospital morgue, while the injured rider was rushed to the University College Hospital (UCH), Ibadan,” he said. Meanwhile, Mrs Abimbola Faniyi, the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) Public Relations Officer in the state, said efforts were underway to obtain the deceased’s details, including her Place of Primary Assignment (PPA). items.title: Ponte d’une tortue verte à Mahdia | Un événement écologique rare sur les côtes tunisiennes
items.description: ​Un événement écologique d’une rare importance a été observé sur les côtes tunisiennes : le nidification d'une tortue verte (Chelonia mydas) a été confirmé sur la plage de Ghedhabna, dans le gouvernorat de Mahdia. ​C'est ce qu'a fait savoir le Tunisian Sea Turtle Rescue Centre (INSTM), en rappelant qu'il s'agit du deuxième enregistrement documenté de ponte pour cette espèce en Tunisie, le premier ayant été observé sur la plage de Rejiche, également dans la région de Mahdia, en 2019. ​Cette découverte majeure est le fruit d'une collaboration étroite entre l'équipe de terrain de l'Institut National des Sciences et Technologies de la Mer (INSTM), sous la supervision du Dr Olfa Chaieb, l'association environnementale Notre Grand Bleu et des riverains, ajoute le communiqué qui rend hommage aux habitants locaux, Abdelmajid Rouine et Sahbi Ismail, pour leur contribution précieuse à la protection de ce site. ​La présence de ce nid souligne la nécessité de poursuivre la recherche scientifique et le suivi sur le terrain afin d'identifier les nouveaux sites de nidification et de comprendre les facteurs modifiant la répartition des tortues marines sous l'effet du réchauffement climatique, indique encore l'INSTM, en affirmant que cet événement met en lumière le rôle indispensable du travail conjoint entre scientifiques, ONG écologistes et communautés locales pour assurer la sauvegarde des espèces menacées. L’article Ponte d'une tortue verte à Mahdia | Un événement écologique rare sur les côtes tunisiennes est apparu en premier sur Kapitalis .

items.title: Département de l’environnement : « nous œuvrons à transformer la ville de Benichab en une cité verte »
items.description: La ministre mauritanienne de l’Environnement et du Développement durable, Messouda mint Baham Mohamed Laghdaf, a déclaré que son ministère travaillait à « l’élaboration d’un programme intégré » visant à mettre en œuvre les directives du président Mohamed Ould Cheikh El Ghazouani, formulées lors de sa visite à la ville de Benichab, et axées sur la végétalisation de la ville. La ministre s’exprimait lundi à Nouakchott, alors qu’elle présidait une réunion rassemblant les chargés de mission, les conseillers techniques, l’inspectrice générale, les directeurs centraux, les coordinateurs de projets et les directeurs des institutions relevant du secteur. Selon la ministre, ce programme comprend « la lutte contre l’avancée du sable, l’amélioration des conditions de vie des habitants, la protection des ressources naturelles, ainsi que l’intensification des efforts en matière d’assainissement en général et de nettoyage de la plage ». Lors de sa visite en Inchiri en septembre dernier, Ould Ghazouani avait déclaré que la ville de Benichab donnait l’espoir « qu’il est possible de résoudre le problème de la propreté dans nos villes et de leur donner un aspect urbain digne, à condition de faire preuve de volonté et d’initiative ». Depuis Benichab, il a lancé « un appel à tous les citoyens, élus et acteurs de la société civile en faveur d’un élan national pour résoudre le problème des déchets » dans les villes.

Ligue 1: Ait Boudlal prolonge à Rennes jusqu'en juin 2028
items.description: Le défenseur international marocain Abdelhamid Ait Boudlal s'apprête à prolonger son contrat avec le Stade Rennais FC, auquel il est lié jusqu'en juin 2028, rapporte lundi le site spécialisé Foot Mercato. « Un accord a été trouvé pour sa prolongation après plusieurs semaines de discussions entre le club et le jeune joueur de 20 ans », souligne le média français, sans préciser la durée de prolongation de l’ancien pensionnaire de l'Académie Mohammed VI de football. Selon Foot Mercato, Ait Boudlal, titulaire à quatre reprises depuis le début de la saison 2026-2027 (280 minutes de jeu), reste l'un des éléments sur lequel comptent les « Rouge et Noir » pour les saisons à venir. Courtisé lors du dernier mercato estival notamment par le club anglais Fulham, le défenseur central a finalement fait le choix de poursuivre son aventure avec le club breton qui a, jusqu'ici, résisté aux tentatives de recrutement de son jeune défenseur en pleine montée en puissance. Cette prolongation devrait lui permettre d'aborder plus sereinement la suite de la saison et de retrouver une place régulière dans les plans de l’entraineur rennais Franck Haise. Abdelhamid Aït Boudlal avait rejoint Rennes en provenance de l'Académie Mohammed VI en juillet 2024 dans le cadre d'un contrat courant jusqu’en 2028. Il a disputé 21 rencontres toutes compétitions confondues lors de la saison 2025-2026, inscrivant deux buts. Avant sa convocation pour l'équipe A du Maroc ces derniers mois, il a évolué dans la sélection marocaine U17 avec laquelle il a atteint la finale de la CAN 2023 et a été classé, alors, parmi les 60 plus grands espoirs du football mondial par The Guardian. items.title: Décès en garde à vue d’un individu arrêté pour trafic de crack à Yoff : la Police livre les premiers éléments de l’autopsie
items.description: Interpellé pour trafic de crack à Yoff, à la suite de la saisie de 28 pierres de cette substance, un individu est décédé en garde à vue dans sa cellule le samedi 10 octobre 2026 vers 4 h du matin. Selon un communiqué rendu public lundi par la Police, les premiers éléments de l’autopsie évoquent un décès consécutif à une lésion d'infarctus aigu du myocarde subcirconférentiel, associée à une cardiomyopathie hypertrophique avec foie cardiaque. Dans le cadre d'une opération antidrogue menée à Yoff par l'Office central de répression du trafic illicite des stupéfiants (OCRTIS), deux individus ont été interpellés pour détention et trafic de crack, à la suite de la saisie de 28 pierres de cette substance. A lire aussi : Arnaque au Mobile Money : la Police nationale tire la sonnette d’alarme Placé en garde à vue au commissariat de l'Unité 15, explique la Police sénégalaise, l'un des mis en cause a été découvert inerte dans sa cellule le samedi 10 octobre 2026, vers 4 h du matin. Les sapeurs-pompiers, promptement requis, sont intervenus sur place avant de l'évacuer vers une structure hospitalière, où son décès a été formellement constaté. « L'autopsie conclut à un décès consécutif à une lésion d'infarctus aigu du myocarde subcirconférentiel, associée à une cardiomyopathie hypertrophique avec foie cardiaque. Des prélèvements toxicologiques et histopathologiques ont été effectués afin de compléter les investigations médicales. L'enquête ouverte suit son cours », informe la même source. M. DIEME

items.title: NDC sinking Ghana’s democracy with Emelia Agbenyo’s appointment – Miracles Aboagye
items.description: The Communications Director of the New Patriotic Party (NPP), Dennis Miracles Aboagye, has accused the National Democratic Congress (NDC) of undermining Ghana’s democracy over the appointment of Emelia Agbenyo as a Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission (EC). He argues that Ms Agbenyo’s alleged political affiliations and previous roles linked to the NDC raise concerns about her ability to discharge her duties independently. Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story on Monday, October 12, Mr Aboagye described the decision as a threat to the democratic principles of neutrality and accountability, which he said were essential to the work of the Electoral Commission. “It’s a shame how low they are sinking this democracy that we’ve all been fighting for and working towards its growth,” he said. “This lady is not just an advocate of the NDC. In fact, he is a die-in-the-wool NDC, even more NDC than Rashid Tanko himself. Are you aware that this lady was a special assistant to Honourable Ayariga when he was Deputy Education Minister during the John Mahama number one presidency? “Is that the role for consultants? Is that a role for neutral people? That is not all. This is a lady who currently holds a political appointment, a partisan political appointment.” Mr Aboagye also referred to a political message attributed to Ms Agbenyo in support of John Mahama during the 2020 and 2024 election campaigns, which he said raised questions about her suitability for a position requiring independence. “This is a lady that is being sold to us as somebody that can independently bear the affairs of our election, except a person who has openly taken sides,” he said. He questioned why the NDC would nominate someone whose political history, in his view, could undermine public confidence in the Electoral Commission. Mr Aboagye maintained that the appointment could affect perceptions of the Commission’s impartiality, insisting that “individuals appointed to oversee elections must be seen to be independent of partisan interests.” His comments follow criticism of Ms Agbenyo’s appointment, with questions being raised about whether her previous political roles are compatible with the neutrality expected of a Deputy Chairperson of the Electoral Commission.

items.title: Ronaldo Asian Champions League match delayed due to missile alert
items.description: Cristiano Ronaldo’s Al Nassr saw their Asian Champions League match against Neftchi Fergana delayed by an hour on Monday after the Saudi-led military coalition said it had intercepted a missile fired by the Houthis towards Riyadh. Saudi Arabia has recently come under a series of attacks from the Iran-backed group, including strikes on oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs — including a string of lethal hits on Riyadh’s international airport. There was a sparse crowd in the stands of Al-Awal Park for the game which was scheduled for 9:15 pm local time (1815 GMT). The stadium announcer said the situation was safe, that the match would be played, and asked spectators to remain in their seats. However, the television channel broadcasting the match announced a one-hour delay. Shortly before, AFP correspondents reported hearing explosions in Riyadh. At the same time, Riyadh residents received an alert on their phones stating: “The region is exposed to a hostile aerial threat. Please remain calm and stay at home or in a safe place, away from windows and doors, and continue to follow civil defense instructions.” Subsequently, the coalition announced the “interception and destruction” of a ballistic missile fired by the Houthis, in a statement on X. This incident did not seem to upset Ronaldo, who scored the 981st goal of his career just before halftime, as the Saudi champions secured a 3-1 win. items.title: Seedorf back in football as Corinthians head coach
items.description: Corinthians have appointed Clarence Seedorf as their head coach, with the former Netherlands midfielder taking on his first coaching role since 2019. The 50-year-old has joined the club on a contract until the end of 2027, with the club 16th in the Brazilian top flight, one place above the relegation zone with eight games left. Seedorf succeeds former Brazil interim national coach Fernando Diniz, who was sacked by Corinthians last week after the club lost seven consecutive league games. Seedorf’s last coaching role was with the Cameroon national team more than seven years ago, and he has previously had underwhelming spells at AC Milan, Shenzhen FC, and Deportivo La Coruña. “Taking on this challenge is an honour, but also a huge responsibility. I am here to give my all and build a team that fights for every ball, every minute, every victory,” said Seedorf of his Corinthians appointment. Seedorf inherits a Corinthians squad which features former Manchester United players Memphis Depay and Jesse Lingard. Dutch great Seedorf retired from playing in 2014 following a glittering career that yielded four Champions League titles, two with AC Milan, one with Real Madrid, and one with Ajax. Seedorf remains the only player to win the Champions League with three different clubs.

items.title: $1bn military arms was never paid into private accounts – Buratai
items.description: Former Chief of Army Staff, retired Lt.-Gen. Tukur Buratai, has clarified that the one billion dollars earmarked for military arms procurement during his time was never paid into individual service accounts. Buratai made the clarification while delivering a keynote lecture at the Defence Correspondents Association of Nigeria (DECAN) Conference and Awards Ceremony on Monday in Abuja. He addressed the controversy surrounding the arms procurement funding as part of his presentation on technology, intelligence-led operations and Nigeria’s national security. The former army chief said the clarification was important in understanding the administration and handling of the funds. He argued that discussions on defence procurement should be grounded in accurate information about funding channels and institutional responsibilities. Buratai’s remarks came amid broader discussions on the need to strengthen Nigeria’s military capabilities through modern technology, intelligence sharing and improved operational coordination. He said the country’s security challenges required sustained investment in equipment and systems capable of supporting intelligence-led operations and responses to emerging threats. The retired general also advocated greater use of technology, including artificial intelligence and integrated command systems, to improve surveillance, intelligence analysis and operational decision-making. The conference, themed “Beyond Kinetic Warfare: Harnessing Technology and Intelligence-Led Operations for Nigeria’s National Security,” also featured the launch of DECAN’s maiden magazine, The Defence Correspondent. items.title: Médina de Tunis | Réouverture de la bibliothèque du Diwan après une restauration complète
items.description: La ministre des Affaires culturelles, Amina Srarfi, a présidé la cérémonie de réouverture de la bibliothèque du Diwan, joyau architectural situé au cœur de la Médina de Tunis. L'événement s'est déroulé, ce lundi 12 octobre 2026, en présence du gouverneur de Tunis, Imed Boukhris, ainsi que de plusieurs hauts cadres du ministère et d'experts du patrimoine, indique le département de la Culture en rappelant que cet édifice historique emblématique a bénéficié d'un vaste programme de maintenance et de restauration intégrale, entièrement pris en charge et exécuté par l'Institut National du Patrimoine (INP). Les interventions techniques menées par les équipes spécialisées de l'INP ont permis de traiter l'ensemble des dégradations tout en renforçant la structure du bâtiment via l'assainissement et l'étanchéité, une consolidation structurelle, une restauration minutieuse des revêtements de sol, remise en état des faïences artisanales et une rénovation des menuiseries en bois et remise en service de la fontaine centrale, ainsi qu'une modernisation des équipements, notamment du réseau électrique. « Afin de préserver l'authenticité et l'identité architecturale du monument, les équipes de l'INP ont rigoureusement appliqué les normes internationales de conservation du patrimoine », affirme le ministère en soulignant que grâce à ces travaux d'envergure, la bibliothèque du Diwan fait son retour dans le paysage culturel de la médina, protégée de manière durable pour les générations futures et prête à accueillir de nouveau chercheurs, lecteurs et passionnés d'histoire. items.title: 2027: Wike unites PDP, APC for Tinubu’s victory in FCT
items.description: Key stakeholders from the Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) and the All Progressives Congress (APC) have formed a united political front dedicated to securing President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in 2027. The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Mr Nyesom Wike, unveiled the historic alliance during a stakeholders’ meeting of the Rainbow Coalition in Abuja on Monday, demonstrating cross-party unity. The News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) reports that the coalition brought together serving and former senators, party chairmen, National Assembly candidates, and grassroots leaders of PDP and APC from the six FCT area councils. The party leaders unanimously agreed that Tinubu remains their sole presidential candidate for 2027. Announcing his role as the coordinator and field commander of the president’s re-election campaign in the FCT and Rivers, Wike stressed that shared national objectives must take precedence over traditional party divisions. “I want to let all of you know that we are going to work together. Nobody should say, ‘I am PDP’ or ‘I am APC.’ For the purpose of this election, we are together,” he said. The minister cited the 2024 Edo State governorship election as clear proof that joint cooperation between APC and PDP elements could decisively shape electoral outcomes. According to him, when political stakeholders align behind a singular, compelling goal, party labels become secondary to results. He explained that the primary focus of the coalition is to ensure Tinubu’s victory at the polls. According to him, the participating parties retain the flexibility to navigate other localised contests while remaining fully aligned at the presidential level. Wike said that the coalition anchored its re-election campaign on the tangible achievements of the Tinubu administration across the FCT and the nation. On infrastructure development, Wike cited extensive road construction, school rehabilitations, police station upgrades, and public facility enhancements across all six FCT area councils. He also cited institutional reforms, particularly the creation of the FCT Civil Service Commission, the appointment of an internal Head of Service, and the establishment of dedicated Secretariats for Women Affairs and Youth Development. According to him, the reforms have created opportunities for career progression among FCT civil servants and expanded participation in governance. On economic reforms and security, the minister pointed at Tinubu’s long-term economic restructuring and vocal support for the proposed establishment of state police to strengthen national security. “By establishing this bipartisan framework, the APC and PDP coalition aims to build a formidable political force that unites leaders and residents behind the continued development and leadership of Tinubu in 2027,” he said. Earlier, APC State Chairman in FCT, Mr Ishaku Yamawo, pledged unalloyed support for Wike, declaring him the “pilot and commandant” of the territory’s electoral campaign. Yamawo lauded the minister for bringing political opponents together under one umbrella to drive strategic victory. His counterpart in the PDP, Usman Yahaya, said, “We are in PDP but we are going to support Tinubu’s re-election 100 per cent.” (NAN) The post 2027: Wike unites PDP, APC for Tinubu’s victory in FCT appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Hincapié and Zubimendi injured in post-match training session
items.description: Arsenal manager Mikel Arteta says it is “far from ideal” that Piero Hincapié and Martin Zubimendi were injured in a post-match training session after the Gunners’ 2-1 Premier League win against Leeds . A training session was held after Saturday’s match at Emirates Stadium for players who either did not feature in or did not play the full 90 minutes against Leeds . Ecuador defender Hincapie was carried off by goalkeeper Illan Meslier during the session, and Arteta later confirmed Spain midfielder Zubimendi was also hurt. Hincapie, 24, came on after 82 minutes as Arsenal saw out victory against Leeds , while Zubimendi, 27, was an unused substitute. “We had a training session planned after the match for everyone that didn’t get enough minutes, and in two unfortunate actions we lost two players,” Arteta said in a news conference before Tuesday’s Champions League match against Lille. “They’ll have further scans to see where they are and we’ll have that time frame for how long they are going to be out for.” When asked by the media what could have been done to prevent the injuries, Arteta joked the pair should not have trained. “Never train and they don’t get injured. The consequence of that is when you ask them to play they have no rhythm and no impact in the game,” the Spaniard added. “It’s never happened in seven years I’ve been here. It could happen in the training session the next day. “It’s happened now and hopefully it doesn’t happen again, but what can you do? “If I had a crystal ball, I would just say, ‘Guys, get in the jacuzzi, and I will see you tomorrow’.” Hincapie has made three Premier League appearances off the bench this season but started Arsenal ‘s Champions League win over Napoli last month. Zubimendi has also largely featured as a substitute, making five Premier League appearances from the bench. How did the injuries happen? By Alex Howell , Football reporter Arsenal had planned for the players who did not play a full game or did not get minutes in the 2-1 win to train at the Emirates Stadium, so that the whole squad could have a recovery day on Sunday and then train on Monday. Arteta regularly arranges for the players who have not played a full match to take part in a small-sided game on the pitch, and this is how Hincapie and Zubimendi picked up the injuries. The manager does this so that all players have a similar output while navigating their busy fixture schedules. Arteta, who says it was done to get “everybody in the best rhythm”, said Hincapie’s ankle injury was more serious than Zubimendi’s. Substitute goalkeeper Meslier was seen carrying Hincapie off the pitch on his back, despite staff members being present.
